items.prompt: A codebase defines P[i] as the sum of A[0:i], excluding A[i]. Which expression matches the half-open query [l, r)?
constraints: P has length n + 1 and P[0] = 0.

options.text: P[r] - P[l]
P[l] - P[r]

feedback.reason: The query endpoints are already prefix boundaries: P[r] contains everything before r and P[l] contains everything before l.

blocks.text: Because both the prefix and the query use half-open boundaries, no endpoint translation is needed. Subtracting P[l] from P[r] leaves exactly A[l:r]. Adding one to r would include A[r], while adding one to l would remove A[l]. The formula is determined by the contract, not by a memorized universal pattern.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_r_plus_one_minus_p_l: This is the formula for an inclusive right endpoint [l, r]. Under [l, r), it includes one extra element A[r] when r < n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_r_minus_p_l_plus_one: P[l + 1] includes A[l], so subtracting it omits the first requested element.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_l_minus_p_r: The boundary order is reversed and produces the negative of the half-open range sum.

items.prompt: Which statement is the strongest invariant for preventing off-by-one errors across prefix construction and querying?
constraints: One convention must be documented and used everywhere.
The implementation uses zero-based array indices.

options.text: P[i] may mean inclusive or exclusive depending on the current formula, as long as tests usually pass.
Every P[i] has one stable meaning—such as the aggregate of the first i elements—and all formulas are derived from that meaning.
Sorting the input removes the need to define prefix boundaries.
Treat P[i] as whichever moving-window sum currently ends at i.

feedback.reason: A prefix index is a semantic boundary, not merely an array position; one stable meaning is what makes formulas derivable and reviewable.

blocks.text: If P[i] always means the aggregate before index i, construction, queries, empty ranges, and sentinel handling follow mechanically. Switching meanings between inclusive and exclusive interpretations creates formulas that can appear plausible but disagree at edges. Sortedness and window state do not repair an inconsistent contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.switch_when_convenient: A value cannot simultaneously summarize two different regions. Mixing conventions is the direct source of off-by-one errors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_to_remove_offsets: Sorting changes value order but does not define whether a prefix index includes the current element. Boundary semantics remain necessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_alias: A window endpoint does not identify all elements before i. Reusing the same notation for moving and cumulative state obscures ownership.

items.prompt: Order the engineering steps for establishing and using a prefix index convention safely.
constraints: The chosen contract is P[i] = aggregate of A[0:i].
Score is based on preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Write the meaning of P[i] and the legal boundary domain 0 through n.
Allocate n + 1 entries and initialize the identity at P[0].
Derive P[i + 1] from P[i] and A[i].
Translate each external range shape into the prefix boundary domain.
Test empty, first-element, last-element, and full-array boundaries.

feedback.reason: The semantic contract must precede storage and formulas; edge tests then verify that every layer honors it.

blocks.text: Starting with code before defining P[i] invites accidental convention mixing. Every later step must be derived from the written boundary meaning.

items: Write that P[i] aggregates A[0:i] and that legal boundaries range from 0 through n.
Allocate n + 1 states and set P[0] to the aggregate identity for the empty prefix.
Derive P[i + 1] from P[i] and A[i], preserving the written meaning at the next boundary.
Translate each external range contract into these boundaries—for example, inclusive [l, r] becomes [l, r + 1).
Test empty, first-element, last-element, and full-array ranges to confirm that construction and API translation agree.

blocks.title: Tests confirm the contract
blocks.text: Edge tests can expose disagreement, but they do not define what P[i] means. The semantic contract must precede storage, recurrence, and query formulas.

items.prompt: Under the half-open contract P[i] = sum of A[0:i], what should the query [x, x) return?
constraints: The API permits empty half-open ranges.

options.text: A[x], because both endpoints name the same element.
It is valid only if A is sorted.
0, because P[x] - P[x] cancels the same boundary state.
The sum of the most recent moving window.

feedback.reason: A half-open range with equal boundaries contains no elements, and identical prefix states cancel to the identity.

blocks.text: The notation [x, x) runs from the boundary before element x to that same boundary, so it includes no elements. In P[i] = sum of A[0:i], every P value is a state at a boundary; the sum of [l, r) is P[r] - P[l]. With equal boundaries, P[x] - P[x] = 0.

This is not a special case for the middle of the array: it works for both x = 0 and x = n. The answer A[x] confuses an element index with a range boundary, and would additionally be out of bounds when x = n. Sorting and the state of a previous window are irrelevant.

blocks.title: Check rule
blocks.text: A half-open range [l, r) contains r - l elements. When l = r, its sum is the sum of the empty set: 0.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a_x: The range [x, x) excludes its right endpoint and contains no element. At x = n there is no A[x] at all.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.invalid_unless_sorted: Sortedness has no effect on whether equal half-open boundaries form an empty range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.current_window_sum: The result is defined entirely by the two supplied prefix boundaries, not by prior query state.

items.prompt: A moving-window implementation uses inclusive left and right element indices, while a prefix helper uses half-open boundaries. Which integration is correct?
constraints: The current window contains A[left] through A[right].

options.text: Call it with [left, right), because endpoint conventions are interchangeable.
Sort the current window so inclusive and exclusive endpoints align.
Use P[right] - P[left] and also subtract A[left].
Call the prefix helper with boundaries [left, right + 1), producing P[right + 1] - P[left].

feedback.reason: The inclusive window’s last element maps to the exclusive prefix boundary immediately after it.

blocks.text: Different components may use different legal conventions, but their interface must translate explicitly. Passing right directly would omit A[right]. Sorting does not change endpoint semantics, and ad hoc compensating arithmetic is harder to reason about than a correct boundary conversion.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reuse_same_pair: P[right] stops before A[right], so the inclusive window’s last element is lost. The conventions are not interchangeable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_before_call: Ordering values cannot reconcile inclusive and exclusive endpoint meanings. It also changes window membership by position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.subtract_outgoing_twice: P[right] - P[left] already excludes A[left] from the removed prefix correctly; subtracting it again corrupts the range and still omits A[right].

items.prompt: Does choosing an inclusive or exclusive prefix convention depend on whether A is sorted?
constraints: Queries refer to positions in the current array order.
Either convention may be implemented consistently.

options.text: No. The convention defines index-boundary ownership and is independent of value order.
Yes. Exclusive prefixes require sorted input.
Yes. Unsorted arrays require inclusive prefixes.
The current moving window determines whether the prefix is inclusive.

feedback.reason: Boundary semantics describe which positions are summarized; they do not impose an ordering property on the values.

blocks.text: Both inclusive and exclusive prefixes can be built over arbitrary sequences, including negative and repeated values. The choice affects storage shape, recurrence, and query formula—not whether the values are sorted. Sorting may change the problem’s positional semantics but cannot determine the convention.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exclusive_only_sorted: An exclusive prefix works on any order because it is defined by indices and addition, not monotonicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.inclusive_only_unsorted: Inclusive prefixes also work on sorted or unsorted input. Value order is orthogonal to endpoint inclusion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_decides_sort: A moving window may consume a prefix helper, but it does not redefine the helper’s persistent boundary contract.

items.prompt: For either a consistent inclusive-prefix or exclusive-prefix implementation over n elements, select the asymptotic build time, range-query time, and separate prefix storage.
constraints: Both implementations store one cumulative value per element boundary or element position.
Each query combines a constant number of stored values.

feedback.reason: A coherent endpoint convention changes constants and formulas, not the linear number of stored states or constant query work.

blocks.text: Both common representations visit each of n elements once, performing constant work per element, so build time is O(n). An inclusive layout stores n cumulative entries and an exclusive layout n + 1; both are O(n) separate space. A query reads and combines a constant number of entries, so query time is O(1).

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: Build time is not O(1) or O(log n) because every input contributes, and O(n log n) adds sorting or logarithmic work that neither convention performs. Query time has no search or scan, rejecting O(log n), O(n), and O(n²). Space is not O(1) or O(log n) because one cumulative state is retained per element or boundary, and not O(n²) because the prefix is one-dimensional.

items.prompt: Which 2D design most directly transfers the exclusive-boundary convention used by a one-dimensional n + 1 prefix?
constraints: Matrix queries use inclusive cell coordinates.
The design should avoid negative row or column indices.

options.text: Use an R × C prefix but switch between inclusive and exclusive meanings per query term.
Use an (R + 1) × (C + 1) prefix with a zero row and column, and translate lower-right coordinates by +1 on both axes.
Sort every row and column so padding is unnecessary.
Store only the most recently queried rectangle at P[R][C].

feedback.reason: The identity boundary extends independently along each axis, preserving one half-open geometric meaning for every prefix entry.

blocks.text: The zero row and column represent empty prefixes before the first real row and column. Inclusive (r2, c2) becomes the exclusive boundary (r2 + 1, c2 + 1), exactly mirroring the 1D translation on both axes. Mixed meanings recreate off-by-one and overlap errors rather than removing them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_padding_mixed_indices: An unpadded inclusive representation can be valid, but switching meanings term by term is not. It usually requires explicit boundary branches.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_rows_columns: Sorting changes matrix geometry and has no effect on whether a prefix index denotes an inclusive or exclusive boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_window_corner: One current rectangle is not reusable boundary state and cannot support arbitrary inclusion-exclusion queries.

items.prompt: Why is P[0]=0 a useful invariant for an exclusive one-dimensional prefix array?

options.text: A range beginning at index 0 can use the same subtraction formula as every other range.
It guarantees every input value and every prefix is nonnegative.
It stores A[0] without consuming an input index.
It keeps prefix values sorted for binary search.

feedback.reason: The empty prefix is the exact contribution before index zero, so subtracting it removes nothing.

blocks.text: For [0,r], the formula becomes P[r+1]-P[0]. This avoids a branch that would otherwise treat the left edge separately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.avoid_negative_values: Prefix sums may be negative when input values are negative.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_first_value: P[0] represents no elements; A[0] first appears in P[1].
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_prefixes: Prefix values need not be ordered when inputs can be negative.

items.prompt: For a 2D exclusive prefix matrix, why are two single-axis prefixes added back after subtracting the top and left regions?

options.text: Their shared top-left region was subtracted twice, so it must be added once by inclusion-exclusion.
The two prefixes represent the requested rectangle's bottom and right boundaries.
Adding them guarantees every rectangle sum is positive.
The requested rectangle must be counted twice before division by two.

feedback.reason: Rectangle extraction is inclusion-exclusion: remove the two outside strips, then restore their overlapping outside corner.

blocks.text: For rows [r1,r2) and columns [c1,c2), the formula is P[r2][c2]-P[r1][c2]-P[r2][c1]+P[r1][c1]. The final term is the twice-removed top-left region.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add_boundary: The prefixes represent regions, not merely individual boundaries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.avoid_negative: Rectangle sums can be negative; positivity is not the purpose.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.double_count_target: The target region is included once after cancellation, not twice.

items.prompt: How is an inclusive query [l,r] translated under an exclusive prefix convention?

options.text: Use the prefix boundary after r: P[r+1] - P[l].
Use P[r] - P[l], leaving r included by default.
Use P[r+1] - P[l+1], which excludes l.
Use P[l] - P[r+1].

feedback.reason: Exclusive P[x] stops before x, so the inclusive right endpoint needs the boundary r+1.

blocks.text: The left boundary l already means the contribution before A[l]. Derive both endpoints from what each prefix contains instead of memorizing a formula detached from the convention.

items.prompt: Why does a 2D exclusive prefix matrix usually include an empty top row and left column?

options.text: Rectangles touching the top or left edge can use the same four-boundary formula.
Padding sorts every matrix row before querying.
Padding makes all matrix entries nonnegative.
Each input cell must be stored twice for correctness.

feedback.reason: Zero boundaries represent the contribution before row zero and column zero.

blocks.text: The extra boundaries prevent special cases and make inclusion-exclusion valid for any rectangle within the grid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.double_cells: Padding adds one boundary per axis, not a duplicate cell copy.

items.prompt: Why are half-open ranges convenient for adjacent prefix queries [a,b) and [b,c)?

options.text: The shared boundary b belongs to neither element range, so formulas compose without double-counting.
Both ranges include b, making their union automatically disjoint.
Half-open notation sorts the input indices.
It is valid only for negative array values.

feedback.reason: Half-open intervals partition a sequence cleanly at a shared boundary.

blocks.text: The first range ends before b and the second begins at b. This convention aligns naturally with P[right]-P[left] and avoids endpoint overlap ambiguity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_include_b: That would double-count an element at the shared boundary under an inclusive element convention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: Boundary notation does not sort data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_only: The convention is independent of value signs.

items.prompt: Which test case is especially useful for detecting a prefix-index off-by-one bug?

options.text: Check singleton ranges and ranges beginning at index zero.
Test only long middle ranges, never boundaries.
Sort the array before testing formulas.
Exclude empty and one-element cases because they are not representative.

feedback.reason: Left-edge and singleton queries expose whether the exclusive boundaries are translated correctly.

blocks.text: Also test a full-range query and an empty range if the contract allows it. Boundary-focused examples validate the convention directly.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_middle_only: Middle cases can pass while edge boundaries remain shifted.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_empty: Small cases are precisely where endpoint errors are easiest to reveal.
